quotes.t: I am proud to belong to a religion which has taught the world both tolerance and universal acceptance.
quotes.source: Response to Welcome, Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 11 September 1893

quotes.t: The whole secret of existence is to have no fear. Never fear what will become of you, depend on no one. Only the moment you reject all help are you free.
Neither seek nor avoid, take what comes.
Difficulties in your life do not come to destroy you, but to help you realize your hidden potential and power, let difficulties know that you too are difficult.
God, our Creator, has stored within our minds and personalities, great potential strength and ability. Prayer helps us to tap and develop these powers.
You see, God helps only people who work hard. That principle is very clear.
Every now and then go away, have a little relaxation, for when you come back to your work your judgment will be surer.

The great bird will take its first flight from the back of the great swan, filling the universe with amazement and filling all writings with its fame and bringing eternal glory to the nest where it was born.
quotes.source: Codex on the Flight of Birds

quotes.t: The eye, the window of the soul, is the chief means whereby the understanding can most fully and abundantly appreciate the infinite works of Nature.
There is no such thing as failure. Failure is just life trying to move us in another direction.
The whole point of being alive is to become the person you were intended to be, to grow out of and into yourself again and again.
You are built not to shrink down to less but to blossom into more.
The East is a career.
The world is a wheel, and it will all come round right.
All is mystery; but he is a slave who will not struggle to penetrate the dark veil.
Where, after all, do universal human rights begin? In small places, close to home.
quotes.source: Remarks at the United Nations, 27 March 1958

quotes.t: The future is literally in our hands to mold as we like. But we cannot wait until tomorrow. Tomorrow is now.
Since everybody is an individual, nobody can be you. You are unique. No one can tell you how to use your time. It is yours. Your life is your own. You mold it. You make it.
We run carelessly to the precipice, after we have put something before us to prevent us seeing it.

What a chimera then is man! What a novelty! What a monster, what a chaos, what a contradiction, what a prodigy! Judge of all things, imbecile worm of the earth; depositary of truth, a sink of uncertainty and error; the pride and refuse of the universe!
We desire truth, and find within ourselves only uncertainty. We seek happiness, and find only misery and death.
The thought of suicide is a great consolation: by means of it one gets successfully through many a bad night.
Hope in reality is the worst of all evils because it prolongs the torments of man.
Faith: not wanting to know what is true.
I was not born with a hunger to be free. I was born free — free in every way that I could know.
A man who takes away another man's freedom is a prisoner of hatred, he is locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness.
Freedom is indivisible; the chains on any one of my people were the chains on all of them, the chains on all of my people were the chains on me.
A picture is not thought out and settled beforehand. While it is being done it changes as one's thoughts change.
The artist must know the manner whereby to convince others of the truthfulness of his lies.
In my case a picture is a sum of destructions. I do a picture — then I destroy it.
I believe that we are not real social workers. We may be doing social work in the eyes of the people, but we are really contemplatives in the heart of the world.
The poor are very great people. They can teach us so many beautiful things.
I want you to find the poor here, right in your own home first. And begin love there.
At any street corner the feeling of absurdity can strike any man in the face.
Man is always prey to his truths. Once he has admitted them, he cannot free himself from them.
For if there is a sin against life, it consists perhaps not so much in despairing of life as in hoping for another life and in eluding the implacable grandeur of this life.
Sorrow is a fruit. God does not make it grow on limbs too weak to bear it.
When a woman is talking to you, listen to what she says with her eyes.
Common sense is in spite of, not as the result of education.
As soon as you're born they make you feel small.
Imagine no possessions, I wonder if you can.
God is a concept by which we measure our pain.
Do not do unto others as you would that they should do unto you. Their tastes may not be the same.
The only man who behaved sensibly was my tailor: he took my measure anew every time he saw me, whilst all the rest went on with their old measurements and expected them to fit me.
Imagination is the beginning of creation. You imagine what you desire, you will what you imagine and at last you create what you will.
Time, which sees all things, has found you out.
Grief teaches the steadiest minds to waver.
Time alone reveals the just man; but you might discern a bad man in a single day.
In the hopes of reaching the moon men fail to see the flowers that blossom at their feet.
The great secret of success is to go through life as a man who never gets used up.

No ray of sunlight is ever lost, but the green which it awakes into existence needs time to sprout, and it is not always granted to the sower to see the harvest. All work that is worth anything is done in faith.
There are only two forces that unite men — fear and interest.
You must not fight too often with one enemy, or you will teach him all your art of war.
There are only two forces in the world, the sword and the spirit. In the long run the sword will always be conquered by the spirit.
To stay with that shakiness — to stay with a broken heart, with a rumbling stomach, with the feeling of hopelessness and wanting to get revenge — that is the path of true awakening.
Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over to annihilation can that which is indestructible be found in us.
It is only when we begin to relax with ourselves that meditation becomes a transformative process.
If you want happiness for an hour, take a nap. If you want happiness for a day, go fishing. If you want happiness for a year, inherit a fortune. If you want happiness for a lifetime, help somebody.
A bird does not sing because it has an answer. It sings because it has a song.
The palest ink is better than the best memory.
Time itself is being, and all being is time.
Not till we are lost, in other words not till we have lost the world, do we begin to find ourselves, and realize where we are and the infinite extent of our relations.
It is never right to do wrong or to requite wrong with wrong, or when we suffer evil to defend ourselves by doing evil in return.
India is a geographical and economic entity, a cultural unity amidst diversity, a bundle of contradictions held together by strong but invisible threads.
He who is not a good servant will not be a good master.
The best is the enemy of the good.
Three may keep a secret, if two of them are dead.
A wonderful fact to reflect upon, that every human creature is constituted to be that profound secret and mystery to every other.
The Heart wants what it wants — or else it does not care.
We will have to repent in this generation not merely for the vitriolic words and actions of the bad people but for the appalling silence of the good people.
Selfishness must always be forgiven, you know, because there is no hope of a cure.
It is amazing how complete is the delusion that beauty is goodness.
Compassion is the chief law of human existence.
The role of a writer is not to say what we can all say, but what we are unable to say.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Vol. 5

quotes.t: Paper has more patience than people.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl (20 June 1942)

quotes.t: Differences are not intended to separate, to alienate. We are different precisely in order to realize our need of one another.
When two do the same thing, it is not the same thing after all.
Conviction, were it never so excellent, is worthless till it convert itself into Conduct.
The beauty of the world which is so soon to perish, has two edges, one of laughter, one of anguish, cutting the heart asunder.
Nothing ever becomes real till it is experienced.
quotes.source: Letter to George and Georgiana Keats, 19 March 1819

quotes.t: I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend.
If today were the last day of my life, would I want to do what I am about to do today?
History shows that where ethics and economics come in conflict, victory is always with economics.
One machine can do the work of fifty ordinary men. No machine can do the work of one extraordinary man.
To be free of all authority, of your own and that of another, is to die to everything of yesterday, so that your mind is always fresh, always young, innocent, full of vigour and passion.
What we obtain too cheap, we esteem too lightly.
Vision is the art of seeing things invisible.
Knowledge is of two kinds. We know a subject ourselves, or we know where we can find information upon it.
quotes.source: Boswell, The Life of Samuel Johnson (1775)

quotes.t: Man is the only animal that laughs and weeps; for he is the only animal that is struck with the difference between what things are, and what they ought to be.
quotes.source: Lectures on the English Comic Writers (1819)

quotes.t: Look not mournfully into the past, it comes not back again.
A moment's insight is sometimes worth a life's experience.
quotes.source: The Professor at the Breakfast Table (1859)

quotes.t: There is in every true woman's heart a spark of heavenly fire, which lies dormant in the broad daylight of prosperity; but which kindles up, and beams, and blazes in the dark hour of adversity.
Happiness in this world, when it comes, comes incidentally. Make it the object of pursuit, and it leads us a wild-goose chase, and is never attained.

When you get into a tight place, and everything goes against you till it seems as if you couldn't hold on a minute longer, never give up then, for that's just the place and time that the tide'll turn.
You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
quotes.source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845)

quotes.t: Resist much, obey little.
If a nation expects to be ignorant and free, in a state of civilization, it expects what never was and never will be.
A person may cause evil to others not only by his actions but by his inaction, and in either case he is justly accountable to them for the injury.
Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.
quotes.source: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785)

quotes.t: And gladly would he learn and gladly teach.

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

Geoffrey Chaucer.bio: English poet, author of The Canterbury Tales; often called the father of English literature.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Harriet Beecher Stowe.bio: Harriet Beecher Stowe was an American author and abolitionist whose novel Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) galvanized anti-slavery sentiment in the United States and abroad. She wrote more than 30 books, including novels, travel memoirs and collections of articles.

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.bio: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was an American poet and educator, among the most popular poets of his century. He wrote Paul Revere's Ride, The Song of Hiawatha and Evangeline, and produced the first American translation of Dante's Divine Comedy.

Immanuel Kant.bio: Immanuel Kant was a German philosopher whose Critique of Pure Reason reshaped modern philosophy by examining the limits of human knowledge. His moral philosophy grounded duty in reason and human dignity, and his essays championed enlightenment and perpetual peace.
Immanuel Kant.credit: J. L. Raab, after a painting by Döbler, Public domain

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

John Stuart Mill.bio: John Stuart Mill was an English philosopher and political economist, the most influential liberal thinker of the 19th century. On Liberty defended individual freedom against social coercion, and his Autobiography candidly records his extraordinary education and mental crisis.

Jonathan Swift.bio: Anglo-Irish writer and satirist, author of Thoughts on Various Subjects.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Nathaniel Hawthorne.bio: Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer known for The Scarlet Letter and The House of the Seven Gables. His works explore sin, guilt and the moral history of Puritan New England.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr..bio: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. was an American physician, poet and polymath, and one of the Fireside Poets. He coined the term 'anesthesia' and wrote the popular 'Breakfast-Table' series of essays and poems, including 'Old Ironsides'.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Samuel Johnson.bio: Samuel Johnson was an English writer who compiled the first great Dictionary of the English Language in 1755. Poet, essayist and the most quoted conversationalist of his age, his life was immortalised in Boswell's famous biography.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Thomas Paine.bio: Thomas Paine was an English-born political writer whose pamphlet Common Sense in 1776 galvanised the American Revolution. His Rights of Man defended the French Revolution against Burke, and his works made him one of the most influential pamphleteers in history.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Washington Irving.bio: Washington Irving was an American short-story writer, essayist and historian best known for 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' and 'Rip Van Winkle'. He was among the first American writers to achieve international fame, and also wrote biographies and histories of Spain.

William Hazlitt.bio: William Hazlitt was an English essayist, literary critic and philosopher regarded as one of the greatest essayists in the English language. His collections, including Table-Talk and The Spirit of the Age, profiled the writers and politics of the Romantic era.
